explanation: Capacity-limited stacks make the end behave like a normal stack. PopAt creates an internal gap; moving each following bottom value backward preserves the logical sequence and restores the full-prefix layout. That layout makes future stack indices predictable.
correctness: Represent the logical contents by concatenating small stacks from oldest to newest, each bottom-to-top. Push appends one value and Pop removes its last value. PopAt removes exactly the last value of the selected segment. Moving the next segment's bottom into the gap keeps every other value's relative position; repeating this propagates the gap to the final segment, which is removed if empty. Thus the resulting contents and segmentation obey the contract after every operation.
walkthrough: With capacity 2, pushes 1,2,3,4 create [1,2] and [3,4]. PopAt(0) returns 2, moves 3 into the first stack and leaves [1,3] and [4]. Pop then returns 4 and removes the last small stack; the next Pop returns 3.
timeComplexity: Push and Pop take O(1) amortized time with growable arrays. PopAt takes O(s*capacity) worst-case time in these implementations, where s is the number of affected small stacks; removing a bottom array element shifts its remaining elements.
spaceComplexity: O(n) payload storage, plus O(s) small-stack metadata, for a maximum of n simultaneously stored values.
edgeCases: Capacity one and removal from the first or last stack.
Repeated PopAt operations after rollover change later indices.
Invalid indices and empty operations must not consume a value.
